item.title: A Geocoding Error Detection Method Using Address and Coordinates
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Accurate estimation of positional errors is critical for geocoded data users. However, existing methods typically depend on high‐quality vector datasets or prior knowledge of the input data and the geocoding process, limiting their applicability in data‐restricted environments. This research proposes a novel Geocoding Error Detection Method (GEDM) that evaluates geocoding quality using only commonly available address text and geocoded coordinates after the geocoding process has been completed. Over 10,000 publicly available points of interest (POIs) across four address categories in Nanjing, China, were geocoded by Gaode Map, and ground‐truth errors were obtained by comparison with verified locations. GEDM identifies approximately 70% of geocoding errors under the experimental settings, with particularly strong performance for well‐structured addresses containing complete elements (e.g., street names) and in high‐density areas. By eliminating the need for external high‐precision reference data or platform‐specific information, GEDM offers a practical and scalable solution for large‐scale geocoding quality assessment, particularly in scenarios where external validation data are limited.
item.content:encoded:
ABSTRACT

Accurate estimation of positional errors is critical for geocoded data users. However, existing methods typically depend on high-quality vector datasets or prior knowledge of the input data and the geocoding process, limiting their applicability in data-restricted environments. This research proposes a novel Geocoding Error Detection Method (GEDM) that evaluates geocoding quality using only commonly available address text and geocoded coordinates after the geocoding process has been completed. Over 10,000 publicly available points of interest (POIs) across four address categories in Nanjing, China, were geocoded by Gaode Map, and ground-truth errors were obtained by comparison with verified locations. GEDM identifies approximately 70% of geocoding errors under the experimental settings, with particularly strong performance for well-structured addresses containing complete elements (e.g., street names) and in high-density areas. By eliminating the need for external high-precision reference data or platform-specific information, GEDM offers a practical and scalable solution for large-scale geocoding quality assessment, particularly in scenarios where external validation data are limited.

item.title: Phantom Capacity in Urban Pedestrian Networks: An AI‐Assisted Approach to Functional Walkability Using Street View Imagery and SAM 3
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Pedestrian network data record the width a street is assigned, not the width that can be walked. This study measures phantom capacity, the share of pedestrian‐intended width lost to obstacles, in Konak, İzmir. Corridors were reconstructed from building footprints, SAM 3 masks from Google Street View imagery were projected onto the ground plane with a camera model calibrated against GIS facade lines, and Effective Clear Width (ECW) was defined as the bottleneck of the widest free lateral runs along a 20 m window. Across 557 nodes on 251 streets, 23.0% had < 0.9 m of clear width and 61.9% had at least 1.5 m. About half of the ECW variance lay within streets, and vehicles occupied 70.2% of the obstructed ground; removing them halved the impassable share. Validation was desk‐based (geometric RMSE 3.85 m; segmentation precision 90.2%), and the estimates describe occupancy at one capture per node.
item.content:encoded:
ABSTRACT

Pedestrian network data record the width a street is assigned, not the width that can be walked. This study measures phantom capacity, the share of pedestrian-intended width lost to obstacles, in Konak, İzmir. Corridors were reconstructed from building footprints, SAM 3 masks from Google Street View imagery were projected onto the ground plane with a camera model calibrated against GIS facade lines, and Effective Clear Width (ECW) was defined as the bottleneck of the widest free lateral runs along a 20 m window. Across 557 nodes on 251 streets, 23.0% had < 0.9 m of clear width and 61.9% had at least 1.5 m. About half of the ECW variance lay within streets, and vehicles occupied 70.2% of the obstructed ground; removing them halved the impassable share. Validation was desk-based (geometric RMSE 3.85 m; segmentation precision 90.2%), and the estimates describe occupancy at one capture per node.

item.title: Detecting Intercity Mobility Subsystems via an Ordered Stochastic Block Model and Anisotropic Metrics: Evidence From China's Pre‐Spring Festival Period
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT While directed networks are a focal point in intercity mobility research, there are limited studies quantifying the uncertainty of directionality using network and geometric indicators. To address this limitation, this study proposes a framework using an ordered stochastic block model with a sequential analytical workflow of anisotropic metrics to analyze intercity mobility before China's Spring Festival. Our findings indicate that China's Spring Festival return‐mobility consists of three subsystems with ordered subgroups. Asymmetric intercity flows establish a hierarchical structure, with developed regions positioned at the top and labor‐exporting cities at the bottom. Flows in the South and East China subsystems are predominantly oriented toward the northwest and west‐northwest, respectively, consistent with return migration to inland hometowns. The results demonstrate the efficacy of combining network science with geometric directionality in characterizing complex spatial interactions, offering valuable insights for urban and regional planning.
item.content:encoded:
ABSTRACT

While directed networks are a focal point in intercity mobility research, there are limited studies quantifying the uncertainty of directionality using network and geometric indicators. To address this limitation, this study proposes a framework using an ordered stochastic block model with a sequential analytical workflow of anisotropic metrics to analyze intercity mobility before China's Spring Festival. Our findings indicate that China's Spring Festival return-mobility consists of three subsystems with ordered subgroups. Asymmetric intercity flows establish a hierarchical structure, with developed regions positioned at the top and labor-exporting cities at the bottom. Flows in the South and East China subsystems are predominantly oriented toward the northwest and west-northwest, respectively, consistent with return migration to inland hometowns. The results demonstrate the efficacy of combining network science with geometric directionality in characterizing complex spatial interactions, offering valuable insights for urban and regional planning.

item.title: Micro‐Scale Mapping of Oviposition Activity Using UAV‐Derived Microenvironment Structure: A Case Study of Aedes albopictus
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Fine‐scale oviposition hotspots can be obscured by coarse environmental representations. We evaluated whether UAV‐derived microenvironment structure adds information beyond proximity‐based and Sentinel‐2 representations for mapping Aedes albopictus oviposition hotspots. Using 282 monitoring sites on a Shanghai university campus, we compared Baseline, Sentinel‐2, and UAV predictor configurations with XGBoost and Random Forest under repeated stratified cross‐validation. With XGBoost, the UAV model achieved higher Accuracy (0.80) and Cohen's κ (0.34) than both comparison models, while Sentinel‐2 achieved slightly higher Recall (0.47 vs. 0.42); UAV AUC was 0.64. Under the same 57‐site inspection quota, Precision@20% increased from 0.33 for both comparison models to 0.49 with UAV variables, an approximately 48% relative improvement. SHAP identified fine‐scale land‐cover and structural variables as important predictive contributors. Although overall discrimination remained moderate, UAV‐derived structural information improved fixed‐quota hotspot prioritization, supporting its use as a fine‐scale follow‐up tool in preselected high‐priority areas.
item.content:encoded:
ABSTRACT

Fine-scale oviposition hotspots can be obscured by coarse environmental representations. We evaluated whether UAV-derived microenvironment structure adds information beyond proximity-based and Sentinel-2 representations for mapping Aedes albopictus oviposition hotspots. Using 282 monitoring sites on a Shanghai university campus, we compared Baseline, Sentinel-2, and UAV predictor configurations with XGBoost and Random Forest under repeated stratified cross-validation. With XGBoost, the UAV model achieved higher Accuracy (0.80) and Cohen's κ (0.34) than both comparison models, while Sentinel-2 achieved slightly higher Recall (0.47 vs. 0.42); UAV AUC was 0.64. Under the same 57-site inspection quota, Precision@20% increased from 0.33 for both comparison models to 0.49 with UAV variables, an approximately 48% relative improvement. SHAP identified fine-scale land-cover and structural variables as important predictive contributors. Although overall discrimination remained moderate, UAV-derived structural information improved fixed-quota hotspot prioritization, supporting its use as a fine-scale follow-up tool in preselected high-priority areas.
